case_study_insert.main_stem: GreenTimber Prefabrication (GTP) is a public limited company in the sustainable timber construction sector in coastal British Columbia, employing a workforce of 64. Founded in 2006 by Isla Green, it manufactures timber-frame wall panels for low-carbon housing and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. GTP plans to invest $1,050,000 in a new computer-aided panel-cutting plant using certified reclaimed timber, financed by a $450,000 bank loan and a $600,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $350,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a panel and a selling price of $19.00, and produces 85,000 units a year. GTP faces a skills gap in operating the new cutting machines and timber waste has risen to 6.1% of input.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q2 2025: The panel plant produced 20,400 units last quarter, with timber waste at 6.1% of input, down from 8.3% a year earlier. Customer quality complaints fell from 31 to 18 per month. Average panel changeover time is 26 minutes. Market research of 350 housebuilders found that 71% would pay up to $0.60 more for certified low-carbon panels, and 49% check chain-of-custody certificates before ordering. A skills audit shows 19 of 64 staff cannot yet operate the computer-aided cutting machines; accredited off-the-job courses at the forestry college cost $1,050 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of GreenTimber Prefabrication for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has lifted the base interest rate from 4.00% to 4.75%, raising borrowing costs for firms with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $14.20 to $14.98 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills at labour-intensive panel plants. (3) Wholesale reclaimed-timber and adhesive costs have risen 10.4% year-on-year, construction-cost inflation is 5.9%, and low-carbon housing starts grew 6.3% over the same period.

questions.question_text: GTP raised $600,000 through a share issue for its $1,050,000 cutting plant. Explain two disadvantages for GTP of using a share issue rather than more bank borrowing alongside the $450,000 loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue dilutes existing ownership and control, so Isla Green and current shareholders give up a stake in GTP. Unlike the $450,000 bank loan, which is repaid and then ends, new equity holders may demand dividends and voting rights indefinitely, reducing the rewards from the $19.00 panels and the 85,000-unit output.

Point 2: Equity is usually more expensive than debt over the long term because investors expect a return that reflects the risk of a new $1,050,000 plant, whereas loan interest on a $450,000 facility is contractually fixed. Issuing shares also involves legal and advisory costs and possible delay, which could hold up the computer-aided cutting machines while the 6.1% timber waste and 19 untrained staff remain unresolved. With fixed costs of $350,000 a year, any reduction in contribution from dividend payments would make the 50,000-unit break-even harder to clear. The board must also weigh that a $600,000 share issue permanently gives away a slice of future profits on 85,000 panels, whereas the $450,000 loan ends once repaid.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid disadvantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to GTP's financing mix and operating data.

questions.question_text: GTP wants to reach more low-carbon housebuilders for its certified panels. Consider selling direct to housebuilders, distributing through builders' merchants, or an e-commerce portal. Which should GTP choose for the new cutting plant? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Selling direct to housebuilders: A direct sales team can explain chain-of-custody certification and the low-carbon story to the 49% of 350 surveyed builders who check certificates before ordering, and can negotiate the $0.60 premium that 71% would pay. Direct contact also gives fast feedback on the 18 monthly complaints and on waste levels. However, managing many individual accounts is expensive for a firm with $350,000 fixed costs and a hierarchical structure, and geographic coverage is limited.

Distributing through builders' merchants: Merchants already hold stock close to sites and give GTP nationwide reach without a large salesforce, which suits the 20,400 panels made last quarter and helps absorb 85,000 units of annual output. They also handle small orders. The drawbacks are lower margins because merchants take a cut, and less control over how the certified low-carbon message is presented, which could weaken the $0.60 premium.

E-commerce portal: An online catalogue with downloadable certificates could cut order costs and reach smaller builders cheaply, with measurable enquiries. Yet panels are bulky and buyers expect delivery scheduling and technical advice; a portal alone cannot build the relationships needed for specification decisions, and it does nothing to solve the 6.1% waste problem.

Recommendation: GTP should sell direct to housebuilders. It protects the premium, communicates certification and captures feedback needed to cut waste, which matters for the $1,050,000 investment. Builders' merchants are rejected because their margin demands and weak message control undermine premium positioning; the e-commerce portal is rejected as unsuitable for a bulky, specification-driven product, though it can support direct selling as an ordering tool.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of distribution options with minimal application to GTP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GTP with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GTP with a well-justified recommendation explaining why merchants and e-commerce are rejected.

questions.question_text: GTP has a skills gap on its computer-aided cutting machines and a hierarchical structure. Explain two benefits for GTP of introducing job rotation among its 64 workers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job rotation moves the 64 workers between cutting, assembly and quality checks, so more staff can operate the new computer-aided plant when 19 of them lack machine skills. This reduces the bottleneck caused by the skills gap and protects the 20,400 panels made last quarter, while giving cover when absenteeism strikes the 26-minute changeover process.

Point 2: Rotation broadens skills and reduces repetitive work, raising motivation in a hierarchical structure where promotion prospects may otherwise be narrow. Better-motivated staff are more likely to spot the causes of the 6.1% timber waste and help bring the 18 monthly complaints down. Multi-skilling also cuts reliance on the $1,050 per employee college courses and makes the $1,050,000 investment more flexible as low-carbon housing starts grow 6.3%. Rotation also spreads the 26-minute changeover work more evenly, reducing the chance that one skilled operator becomes a single point of failure on the cutting plant.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GTP's skills gap, waste, complaints and output.

questions.question_text: GTP needs more staff who can run the new cutting machines. Consider recruiting experienced operators externally or retraining existing workers. Which should GTP choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Recruiting experienced operators externally: Hiring skilled machine operators could close the 19-person gap quickly and bring knowledge of other plants, helping the 20,400-panel quarterly output and reducing the 6.1% waste. Recruitment advertising and selection do take time, and new hires need induction into GTP's certified reclaimed-timber standards. External hires are also likely to command higher wages, which matters with the $1,050,000 investment and $350,000 fixed costs to service, and they may not fit the democratic leadership culture.

Retraining existing workers: The forestry college offers accredited courses at $1,050 per employee, so training the 19 untrained staff would cost 19 × $1,050 = $19,950 — small beside the $1,050,000 plant. Existing workers already know GTP's quality standards and certified timber processes, so training fits the current team and supports job rotation. The downside is the time until they are productive, during which the skills gap and 18 monthly complaints may persist.

Decision: GTP should retrain its existing workers. The $19,950 cost is modest, the trainees already understand the business, and the approach strengthens commitment and flexibility on a $1,050,000 asset. External recruitment is rejected because higher pay, longer induction and cultural fit make it slower and riskier for a 64-person plant; GTP can recruit one experienced mentor to accelerate the training rather than hiring the whole team. That keeps the $19,950 training spend modest beside the $1,050,000 plant and protects the $7.00 contribution on 85,000 panels, since existing workers already understand the certified reclaimed-timber standards that 49% of builders check before ordering.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of recruitment and training options with limited application to GTP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in the context of GTP.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a well-justified decision covering cost, speed and fit.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GTP's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $350,000 ÷ ($19.00 − $12.00) = $350,000 ÷ $7.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $19.00 − $12.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GTP's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare 50,000-unit break-even output with 85,000 units produced to confirm a margin of safety of 35,000 units before the $1,050,000 cutting plant is at risk.
2. Use the $7.00 contribution to evaluate the $0.60 premium: if all 85,000 panels gained it, contribution would rise to $7.60, indicating how valuable the 71% of builders willing to pay more are.
3. Plan repayments on the $450,000 bank loan: each panel above 50,000 adds $7.00, so roughly 4,167 panels a month must be sold above break-even to cover the $350,000 annual fixed costs.
4. Monitor unit cost ($350,000 ÷ 85,000 units + $12.00 = $16.12 a panel) against the 6.1% timber waste and 10.4% input inflation in Appendix 3, so management can react quickly to cost drift.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 85,000 units; valuing the $0.60 premium on $7.00 contribution; loan-service targets on $350,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $16.12 for waste and inflation control.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GTP's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has GTP's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 38.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 11.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.5%
ROCE 2024 = 16.5%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: Gross profit 2,100 ÷ revenue 6,000 × 100 = 35.0% in 2024; 2,584 ÷ 6,800 × 100 = 38.0% in 2025. Operating profit 660 ÷ revenue 6,000 × 100 = 11.0%; 850 ÷ 6,800 × 100 = 12.5%. Operating profit 660 ÷ capital employed 4,000 × 100 = 16.5%; 850 ÷ 4,250 × 100 = 20.0%. Revenue rose from 6,000 to 6,800 while cost of sales increased from 3,900 to 4,216, so gross profit grew from 2,100 to 2,584. Capital employed rose from 4,000 to 4,250 as the $1,050,000 plant was added, and interest expense increased from 80 to 90.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, indicating broad progress. The higher trading margin is consistent with 71% of surveyed builders willing to pay $0.60 more for certified low-carbon panels, and operating profit grew faster than revenue, showing control of overheads despite more interest. Returns on the enlarged capital base also rose, which is a good sign while the new cutting plant is still bedding in. Caution is needed because 6.1% timber waste and a skills gap affecting 19 of 64 staff could raise costs later, and the 10.4% rise in reclaimed-timber and adhesive prices may squeeze the next accounting period.

Conclusion: GTP's profitability has improved. Gross and operating margins and returns on capital all increased, so the conclusion is well supported; management should secure the $0.60 premium and close the skills gap to protect it.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States isolated figures with little or no accurate calculation of the three measures.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three measures for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years plus detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on profitability.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GTP of using certified reclaimed timber in its low-carbon wall panels.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Research shows 71% of 350 housebuilders would pay up to $0.60 more for certified low-carbon panels, and 49% check chain-of-custody certificates. Certified reclaimed timber lets GTP charge that premium, lifting contribution from $7.00 toward $7.60 per panel and supporting the $1,050,000 plant's 85,000-unit target. It also aligns with the 6.3% growth in low-carbon housing starts, helping win new specifications and reducing demand for virgin timber.

Disadvantage: Reclaimed timber can contain variability that causes the current 6.1% waste rate and the 18 monthly complaints, and certification requires record-keeping and audits that add cost. If buyers question the consistency of reclaimed panels, the $0.60 premium may not be achieved across all 350 builders, while the 10.4% rise in input prices raises the $12.00 variable cost. Extra inspection could also slow the 26-minute changeover and reduce capacity at the cutting plant. Managers must judge whether the 71% premium outweighs these extra inspection costs across all 85,000 panels, especially while 19 of 64 staff still need training.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to GTP's research data, costs and waste rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.75%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 10.4% rise in input costs will affect GTP. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.00% to 4.75%): If GTP's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage-point rise adds 0.0075 × $450,000 = $3,375 a year (derivation shown). This is minor against $350,000 of annual fixed costs and zero if the loan is fixed. Higher rates may raise the cost of future finance for the $1,050,000 plant, though 6.3% growth in low-carbon housing starts supports sales.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, from $14.20 to $14.98 per hour): GTP employs a workforce of 64 at a labour-intensive panel plant, so the rise increases wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert provides no hours worked and no individual pay rates, so no annual wage total can be honestly computed; the defensible method is qualitative comparison with labour productivity of 85,000 units ÷ 64 workers = 1,328.1 units per worker (arithmetic shown from insert figures). If output per worker falls while 19 staff still need training, unit labour costs will rise and erode the $7.00 contribution from $19.00 less $12.00.

Input cost inflation (10.4%): The insert does not decompose the $12.00 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound can be derived: if all of it rose 10.4%, that is 0.104 × $12.00 = $1.248, about $1.25 a panel; over 85,000 panels this is 85,000 × $1.248 = $106,080 a year. Even a partial pass-through would significantly reduce contribution, and 5.9% construction-cost inflation limits pricing power, although the $0.60 premium valued by 71% of builders offers protection.

Conclusion: The 10.4% rise in input costs will have the greatest impact. It repeats on all 85,000 panels and directly attacks the $7.00 contribution that justifies the $1,050,000 investment, while the interest effect is a conditional $3,375 and the wage effect cannot be quantified from the insert and can be offset by productivity gains. GTP should lock in the premium and negotiate timber supply contracts.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to GTP.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on GTP's costs or financing in context with shown arithmetic where figures are used.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context, with derivations shown and a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
